def: the process plants use to turn sunlight, water and carbon dioxide into sugar, releasing oxygen
why: It supplies the oxygen we breathe and the energy at the base of most food chains.
ex: During photosynthesis, the leaves of the oak tree capture sunlight to make the sugars the tree needs to grow.
Maria showed her son the tiny oxygen bubbles that pondweed releases during photosynthesis on a sunny day.

cloze.s: Kept in a dark closet for weeks, the houseplant could not carry out ___ and slowly turned yellow.

note: Cellular respiration works in the other direction, releasing the energy that this process stores in sugar.

def: the force by which objects with mass pull toward one another, keeping us on the ground
why: It explains why things fall, why the Moon orbits Earth and why planets orbit the Sun.
ex: Kwame dropped his phone, and gravity sent it straight onto the kitchen tiles.
Astronauts on the Moon can jump higher because its gravity is much weaker than Earth's.

cloze.s: The Moon's ___ is the main cause of the rising and falling ocean tides on Earth.

def: the smallest unit of a chemical element, made of a central nucleus surrounded by electrons
why: Everything around us, from air to bones, is built from these tiny particles.
ex: A single drop of water contains an enormous number of hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
In chemistry class, Wei drew an atom with electrons circling a nucleus of protons and neutrons.

cloze.s: A water molecule is made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen ___.

note: An atom is a single unit; a molecule is two or more atoms bonded together.

def: two or more atoms chemically bonded together, forming the smallest unit of a substance such as water
why: Medicines, foods and fuels all work through the shapes and reactions of these particles.
ex: Each molecule of carbon dioxide has one carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms.
Priya's biology teacher built a model of a glucose molecule out of colored balls and sticks.

cloze.s: Oxygen gas in the air exists mostly as a ___ made of two oxygen atoms bonded together.

def: the change of a liquid into a gas, usually at its surface, as when puddles dry up
why: It drives the water cycle and explains why sweating cools the body.
ex: On hot afternoons, evaporation shrinks the puddles on the playground within an hour.
Salt makers rely on evaporation to leave sea salt behind in shallow coastal ponds.

cloze.s: Sweat cools you down because heat is carried away from the skin during ___.

def: a sequence showing which living things eat which, passing energy from plants to animals to predators
why: It shows how harm to one species, such as a decline in insects, can ripple out to many others.
ex: In this food chain, grass feeds rabbits, and rabbits in turn feed foxes.
Diego's class learned that mercury entering a food chain can build up in the animals at the top.

cloze.s: Hawks sit near the top of the ___, eating snakes that eat mice that eat seeds.

note: A food web is the larger network formed by many interlinked food chains.

def: the molecule inside cells that carries the inherited instructions for how a living thing grows and functions
why: It underlies heredity, ancestry and paternity tests, forensic evidence and much of modern medicine.
ex: Hannah sent a saliva sample to a lab to learn what her DNA revealed about her ancestry.
Nearly every cell in your body holds its own complete copy of your DNA, packed tightly into the nucleus.

cloze.s: The structure of ___ is a double helix, shaped like a twisted ladder.

note: Short for deoxyribonucleic acid.

def: the process by which living things with helpful inherited traits survive and reproduce more, so those traits spread
why: It is the main mechanism of evolution described by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace.
ex: Through natural selection, dark-colored peppered moths became more common on soot-covered trees in industrial England.
Doctors worry that overusing antibiotics speeds the natural selection of bacteria that survive the drugs.

cloze.s: In Darwin's theory, ___ means individuals with useful traits leave more offspring, so those traits become common.

note: Not the same as evolution itself; it is one of the main forces that causes evolution.

def: a community of living things interacting with each other and their physical surroundings, like a pond or forest
why: Conservation and environmental decisions are often judged by their effect on these living systems.
ex: A coral reef is a crowded ecosystem where fish, algae and coral depend on one another.
The new dam altered the river ecosystem, blocking salmon from reaching their spawning grounds.

cloze.s: Introducing a foreign predator to the island upset the delicate balance of its ___.

def: how much mass is packed into a given volume, which decides whether something floats or sinks
why: It explains why ice floats, why oil sits on top of water and why hot air rises.
ex: Ice floats on a lake because its density is lower than that of liquid water.
Olga pointed to the different density of oil and vinegar to explain why her salad dressing separated.

cloze.s: A lead ball feels much heavier than a wooden ball of the same size because lead has a greater ___.

def: the force that resists motion when two surfaces rub or slide against each other
why: It lets tires grip the road and shoes grip the floor, but it also wears out machine parts.
ex: Rubbing your hands together creates friction, which warms them on a cold morning.
Icy roads are dangerous because there is so little friction between the tires and the pavement.

cloze.s: Engineers add oil to engines to reduce the ___ between moving metal parts.

note: Also used figuratively for conflict between people, as in "friction on the team."

def: a chart arranging all known chemical elements in rows and columns by atomic number and shared properties
why: It is the central reference of chemistry, letting scientists predict how elements will behave.
ex: Malik memorized the first twenty elements of the periodic table before his chemistry exam.
Dmitri Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table for elements that had not yet been discovered.

cloze.s: Hydrogen sits in the top-left corner of the ___ as element number one.

def: a section of DNA carrying instructions for a particular protein or trait, passed from parents to children
why: It helps explain inherited traits, family health risks and the results of DNA testing.
ex: A single gene strongly influences whether a person can taste certain bitter compounds.
Doctors tested Fatima for a gene variant linked to a higher risk of breast cancer.

cloze.s: Eye color is shaped by more than one ___, which is why siblings can have different eye colors.

note: A gene is one unit of heredity; the genome is an organism's complete set of DNA.

def: a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself
why: These substances make much of industry and car exhaust cleaning work, and enzymes are the body's own versions.
ex: A car's catalytic converter uses metals such as platinum as a catalyst to clean exhaust gases.
An enzyme in saliva acts as a catalyst, starting to break down starch as soon as you chew.

cloze.s: Adding a ___ made the reaction finish in minutes instead of days, and the substance was recovered unchanged.

note: Figuratively, a person or event that triggers change: "The report was a catalyst for reform."

def: the time needed for a radioactive substance, or a drug in the body, to fall to 50 percent of its amount
why: It is used to date ancient objects with carbon-14 and to decide how often medicines must be taken.
ex: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, which lets scientists date ancient bones.
Because the drug has a short half-life, Yuki's doctor told her to take it twice a day.

cloze.s: After one ___, only 50 grams remained of the original 100 grams of the radioactive isotope.

def: the capacity to do work that an object has because it is moving, increasing with its mass and speed
why: It explains why doubling a car's speed gives it four times as much destructive power in a crash.
ex: A roller coaster gains kinetic energy as it plunges down the first big hill.
Wind turbines capture the kinetic energy of moving air and convert it into electricity.

cloze.s: As the bowling ball sped down the lane, its ___ grew until it scattered the pins on impact.

note: Contrast potential energy, which is stored energy due to position, such as water held behind a dam.

def: a well-tested explanation of some part of nature, supported by a large body of evidence
why: Knowing it shows why calling evolution or gravity "just a theory" misreads what scientists mean.
ex: Germ theory is a scientific theory explaining that many diseases are caused by microorganisms.
Aisha explained that a scientific theory is not a guess but an explanation backed by many experiments.

cloze.s: Evolution is a ___, meaning a broad explanation confirmed by many independent lines of evidence.

note: Not the everyday sense of "theory" as a hunch; a hypothesis is the testable proposal that comes first.

def: one of two or more forms of the same chemical element whose atoms have different numbers of neutrons
why: These forms are used in carbon dating, medical scans, cancer treatment and nuclear power.
ex: Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope that archaeologists use to date ancient wood and bone.
Hospitals use a radioactive isotope of iodine to diagnose and treat certain thyroid conditions.

cloze.s: Uranium-235 is the ___ of uranium used to fuel most nuclear power plants.

def: a measure of a system's disorder, which naturally tends to increase over time in an isolated system
why: It explains why heat flows from hot to cold and why many processes cannot run in reverse.
ex: An ice cube melting in a warm drink is a familiar example of entropy increasing.
Liam joked that entropy explains why his tidy desk always drifts back toward clutter.

cloze.s: According to the second law of thermodynamics, the ___ of an isolated system never decreases.

note: Figuratively used for a gradual slide into disorder or decline.

def: the movement of water through a membrane from a weaker solution into a more concentrated one
why: It explains how cells and plant roots take in water and why salt draws moisture out of food.
ex: Through osmosis, the wilted celery stalk soaked up water overnight and became crisp again.
Salting sliced eggplant pulls water out of it by osmosis before cooking.

cloze.s: Red blood cells placed in pure water swell and can burst as water rushes in by ___.

note: Figuratively, absorbing knowledge gradually and without effort: "She learned the slang by osmosis."

def: a scale, usually 0 to 14, showing how acidic or alkaline a solution is, with 7 as neutral
why: It matters for swimming pools, garden soil, digestion and blood chemistry.
ex: Lemon juice has a low pH, around 2, which makes it strongly acidic.
Tomás tested the soil's pH before planting blueberries, which prefer acidic ground.

cloze.s: Human blood is kept within a narrow ___ range of about 7.35 to 7.45.

note: Each step on the scale is a tenfold change: pH 3 is ten times as acidic as pH 4.

def: the full range of radiation, from radio waves and microwaves through visible light to X-rays and gamma rays
why: It connects radios, microwave ovens, rainbows, sunburn and medical X-rays as forms of the same phenomenon.
ex: Visible light is only a tiny slice of the electromagnetic spectrum that our eyes can detect.
Telescopes that observe across the electromagnetic spectrum reveal details invisible to the human eye.

cloze.s: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths in the ___, while gamma rays have the shortest.

def: the principle that whenever one object pushes on another, it is pushed back equally hard in the opposite direction
why: It explains how rockets fly, swimmers move forward and people jump by pushing against something.
ex: Rockets rely on Newton's third law: hot gases blast downward, and the rocket is pushed upward.
When Jamal pushed off the pool wall, Newton's third law sent him gliding forward.

cloze.s: A balloon zooming forward as air rushes out the back is a classic demonstration of ___.

note: Often summarized as "for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction."

def: a close, long-term relationship between two different species, often benefiting both
why: It explains partnerships like bees and flowers, and the gut bacteria that help humans digest food.
ex: Clownfish and sea anemones live in symbiosis, each helping protect the other from predators.
Cows depend on symbiosis with microbes in their stomachs to digest tough grass.

cloze.s: A lichen is an example of ___, a partnership between a fungus and algae living as one.

note: In biology it can include relationships where one partner is harmed; in everyday speech it usually means mutual benefit.

def: Einstein's account of how space, time, motion and gravity are linked, including that time slows at very high speeds
why: It underpins GPS accuracy, the equation E = mc² and our understanding of black holes.
ex: GPS satellites must correct their clocks for effects predicted by the theory of relativity.
Sofia's physics professor said the theory of relativity changed how scientists think about space and time.

cloze.s: Einstein's ___ includes the famous equation E = mc², linking mass and energy.

note: Includes special relativity (1905) and general relativity (1915), which describes gravity as curved spacetime.

def: the branch of physics describing how matter and light behave at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles
why: It explains how lasers, transistors and MRI machines work, though its predictions often seem strange.
ex: Quantum mechanics shows that electrons can behave both like particles and like waves.
The engineer said modern computer chips could not be designed without quantum mechanics.

cloze.s: At the scale of single atoms, everyday physics breaks down and ___ is needed to predict behavior.

def: the lowest temperature theoretically possible, minus 273.15 °C or minus 459.67 °F, where particle motion is minimal
why: It is the starting point of the Kelvin scale and a limit scientists approach but never reach.
ex: Scientists have cooled atoms to within a tiny fraction of a degree of absolute zero.
The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, so no temperature in kelvins is ever negative.

cloze.s: The coldest temperature physically possible, 0 on the Kelvin scale, is called ___.

def: invisible material, detected only through its gravity, that astronomers estimate outweighs ordinary visible material about five to one
why: Explaining what it is remains one of the biggest unsolved problems in physics and astronomy.
ex: Galaxies spin so fast that astronomers believe dark matter must supply extra gravity to hold them together.
Researchers built detectors deep underground hoping to catch a particle of dark matter.

cloze.s: Because galaxies rotate faster than their visible stars can explain, scientists propose large amounts of unseen ___.

note: Not the same as dark energy, the proposed cause of the universe's accelerating expansion.

def: the study of how chemical tags on DNA turn instructions on or off without changing the underlying sequence
why: It helps explain how diet, stress and environment can influence health without rewriting DNA.
ex: Identical twins can grow more different over time, partly because of epigenetics.
Kenji's research in epigenetics looks at how early nutrition affects disease risk later in life.

cloze.s: Though they share identical DNA, a liver cell and a skin cell behave differently largely because of ___.

def: the change in pitch or frequency of a wave as its source moves toward or away from an observer
why: It explains a passing siren's changing sound and is used in weather radar, ultrasound and astronomy.
ex: The Doppler effect makes an ambulance siren sound higher as it approaches and lower as it drives away.
Weather forecasters use radar based on the Doppler effect to detect rotating winds inside storms.

cloze.s: Astronomers use the ___ to detect planets around distant stars, which wobble slightly toward and away from Earth.

def: the body's network of cells, tissues and organs that defends against germs and other invaders
why: It explains how we fight infections, how vaccines work and why some people get sicker than others.
ex: A healthy immune system usually clears a common cold within a week or two.
Patients who take certain drugs after an organ transplant have a weakened immune system.

cloze.s: White blood cells are key soldiers of the ___, attacking bacteria and viruses.

def: a preparation that trains the body's defenses to recognize a germ, protecting against future infection or serious illness
why: These shots prevent diseases such as measles and polio and are central to public health.
ex: Diego got a flu vaccine at the pharmacy before winter arrived.
The polio vaccine helped make the disease rare in most of the world.

cloze.s: Before her trip, Priya visited a travel clinic to get the ___ that protects against yellow fever.

note: Vaccination is the act of giving one; immunity is the protection that results.

def: the push of circulation against the walls of the arteries, recorded as top and bottom numbers like 120/80
why: Persistently high readings raise the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease, often without symptoms.
ex: The nurse wrapped a cuff around Hannah's arm to check her blood pressure.
Cutting back on salt helped Malik lower his blood pressure over several months.

cloze.s: High ___ is called a "silent killer" because it often causes no symptoms until damage is done.

note: The top (systolic) number is measured as the heart beats; the bottom (diastolic) number is between beats.

def: a unit measuring the energy that food provides to the body or that physical activity uses up
why: Food labels list them, and balancing intake against use helps explain weight gain or loss.
ex: Liam checked the label to see how many calories were in the granola bar.
A long bike ride on the weekend can burn several hundred calories.

cloze.s: The nutrition label showed that one slice of the frozen pizza contains about 300 ___.

note: Food "calories" are actually kilocalories, each equal to 1,000 small calories.

def: a microscopic germ that can multiply only inside living cells, causing illnesses like colds and flu
why: Knowing how they spread explains why antibiotics do not cure colds and why handwashing helps.
ex: The common cold is caused by a virus, so antibiotics will not help.
Aisha stayed home so she would not spread the stomach virus to her coworkers.

cloze.s: Measles is caused by a ___, which is why antibiotics cannot cure it.

note: Much smaller than bacteria and unaffected by antibiotics. A computer virus is a separate, borrowed sense.

def: the rhythmic throb of the arteries with each heartbeat, often felt at the wrist or neck
why: Checking it gives a quick measure of heart rate, used in first aid, fitness and medical exams.
ex: The coach taught us to find our pulse at the wrist right after sprinting.
A normal resting pulse for adults is roughly 60 to 100 beats per minute.

cloze.s: The paramedic pressed two fingers to the side of Jamal's neck to check his ___.

def: a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing, used to treat bacterial infections
why: Using them correctly matters because they do not work on viruses, and overuse breeds resistant germs.
ex: The doctor prescribed an antibiotic for Sofia's strep throat.
Penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, became the first widely used antibiotic.

cloze.s: Strep throat is a bacterial infection, so the doctor prescribed an ___.

def: all the chemical processes in the body that turn food into energy and build or repair tissues
why: It helps explain differences in energy needs and how age and muscle mass affect weight.
ex: Muscle burns more energy at rest than fat does, so strength training can modestly raise metabolism.
Many medicines are broken down by metabolism in the liver before they leave the body.

cloze.s: Thyroid hormones help control the body's ___, so an underactive thyroid can cause tiredness and weight gain.

def: a waxy, fat-like substance in the blood that cells need but that can build up in arteries when too high
why: High LDL levels raise the risk of heart attack and stroke, so it is checked in routine blood tests.
ex: Wei's doctor ordered a blood test to check his cholesterol levels.
Statins are drugs that lower cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart disease.

cloze.s: LDL, often called "bad" ___, can form plaques that narrow the arteries.

note: The liver makes much of the body's supply, so diet is only part of the story.

def: a nutrient group, including sugars, starches and fiber, that is the body's main source of quick energy
why: Bread, rice, fruit and pasta are rich in them, and they matter for diabetes care and diet planning.
ex: Before the marathon, Kwame ate pasta and rice to load up on carbohydrates.
People with diabetes often count the carbohydrates in each meal to manage their blood sugar.

cloze.s: Potatoes, bread and rice are all rich in the nutrients called ___.

def: an overreaction of the body's defenses to a normally harmless substance like pollen, peanuts or pet dander
why: Reactions range from mild sneezing to life-threatening anaphylaxis, so they matter for food, medicine and school safety.
ex: Because of her peanut allergy, Yuki carries an epinephrine auto-injector everywhere she goes.
Every spring, Tomás takes medicine for his pollen allergy.

cloze.s: Hannah sneezes and gets itchy eyes around cats because she has an ___ to their dander.

note: Not the same as an intolerance, such as lactose intolerance, which does not involve the immune system.

def: a harmful shortage of water in the body, caused by losing more fluid than you take in
why: It is common in heat, exercise and illness, and can be dangerous for babies and older adults.
ex: After hiking all day in the desert, Diego felt dizzy from dehydration.
Severe diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration in young children.

cloze.s: Medics treated the marathon runner for ___ by giving her fluids through an IV.

def: the ability of bacteria to survive drugs designed to kill them, often driven by overuse of those drugs
why: Health agencies call it a major global threat because common infections can become hard to treat.
ex: MRSA is a staph infection known for its antibiotic resistance.
Farmers were urged to limit drug use in livestock to slow antibiotic resistance.

cloze.s: Doctors avoid prescribing bacteria-killing drugs for viral colds partly to slow the spread of ___.

note: It is the bacteria, not the patient, that become resistant.

def: community-wide protection that arises when so many people are protected against a disease that it struggles to spread
why: It shields people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns or those with weakened defenses.
ex: Measles is so contagious that herd immunity is estimated to require about 95 percent of people to be immune.
Thanks to herd immunity, the baby was protected even before she was old enough for the vaccine.

cloze.s: When nearly everyone at a school is vaccinated, ___ helps protect the few students who cannot get the shot.

def: a hormone made by the pancreas that lets cells absorb sugar from the blood
why: It is central to diabetes, in which the body makes too little of it or responds poorly to it.
ex: People with type 1 diabetes must take insulin because their pancreas makes little or none.
After a meal, rising blood sugar signals the pancreas to release insulin.

cloze.s: In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the pancreas cells that produce ___.

def: the body's protective response to injury or infection, causing redness, heat, swelling and pain
why: In the short term it helps healing, but long-lasting forms are linked to arthritis, heart disease and other conditions.
ex: Ice and rest reduced the inflammation in Olga's sprained ankle.
Ibuprofen can ease inflammation and the pain that comes with it.

cloze.s: The red, swollen, warm skin around the splinter was a sign of ___.

def: a screening number from a person's weight divided by the square of their height, used to estimate weight category
why: Doctors use it as a quick screen, though it does not measure body fat directly or account for muscle.
ex: Malik's body mass index came out high, but his doctor noted that much of his weight was muscle.
For adults, a body mass index from 18.5 to 24.9 is classified as the healthy weight range.

cloze.s: To calculate ___, divide weight in kilograms by height in meters squared.

def: a chemical messenger made by glands and carried in the blood to control processes like growth and mood
why: Many conditions, from diabetes to thyroid disorders, come down to too much or too little of one.
ex: Adrenaline is a hormone that prepares the body to react quickly in an emergency.
Melatonin is a hormone that helps regulate the sleep cycle.

cloze.s: The thyroid gland releases a ___ into the blood that helps control how fast the body uses energy.

def: an illness in which the body's defenses mistakenly attack its own healthy tissues
why: Conditions such as type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus fall into this group.
ex: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease that attacks the lining of the joints.
Fatima's doctor explained that celiac disease is an autoimmune disease triggered by gluten.

cloze.s: In multiple sclerosis, an ___, the body attacks the protective coating of its own nerves.

def: any germ, such as a virus, bacterium, fungus or parasite, that can cause disease
why: Public health, food safety and hospital hygiene all focus on stopping these from spreading.
ex: Salmonella is a pathogen often linked to undercooked chicken and eggs.
Hospital staff change gloves between patients to avoid passing a pathogen from one person to another.

cloze.s: Boiling water for one minute kills just about any ___ that could make you sick.

def: the body's internal clock, a roughly 24-hour cycle that regulates sleep, alertness and hormones
why: It explains jet lag, the health effects of night-shift work and why sleep timing matters.
ex: Flying from Chicago to Tokyo threw off Priya's circadian rhythm for several days.
Bright screens late at night can delay your circadian rhythm and make it harder to fall asleep.

cloze.s: Jet lag happens because your ___ is still set to the time zone you left.

def: a chemical messenger that carries signals between nerve cells, such as dopamine or serotonin
why: Many medications for depression, Parkinson's disease and pain work by changing their levels.
ex: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter involved in mood, sleep and digestion.
Parkinson's disease involves the loss of brain cells that make the neurotransmitter dopamine.

cloze.s: Dopamine is a ___ released across the tiny gap between two nerve cells.

def: a Y-shaped protein made by white blood cells that latches onto a specific germ to mark or neutralize it
why: Vaccines, blood tests for past infection and some modern drugs all depend on them.
ex: Sofia's blood test showed antibody levels high enough to protect her against hepatitis B.
A blood test detected an antibody showing that Liam had been infected with the virus in the past.

cloze.s: Some cancer drugs are lab-made versions of an ___ designed to latch onto tumor cells.

note: Not the same as an antigen, the foreign molecule that an antibody recognizes.

def: the body's ability to keep internal conditions like temperature and blood sugar stable despite outside changes
why: Many illnesses can be understood as a breakdown in this balancing act.
ex: Sweating on a hot day is part of homeostasis, keeping body temperature steady.
The kidneys help maintain homeostasis by balancing water and salt in the blood.

cloze.s: Shivering in the cold is one way the body maintains ___, generating heat to keep its temperature steady.

def: a second disease or condition present at the same time as a person's main illness
why: Doctors and researchers weigh these because they affect treatment choices and outcomes.
ex: Diabetes is a common comorbidity in patients with heart disease.
The researchers recorded each patient's main comorbidity, such as obesity or kidney disease.

cloze.s: Diego's kidney disease was a ___ that made treating his heart condition more complicated.

def: the study of how diseases spread, who gets them and what factors raise or lower risk in populations
why: It is how we learned that smoking causes lung cancer and how outbreaks are tracked and controlled.
ex: Epidemiology showed that contaminated water, not bad air, spread cholera in 1850s London.
Aisha studied epidemiology so she could help her city track outbreaks of foodborne illness.

cloze.s: John Snow's map of cholera deaths around a London water pump is a founding moment in ___.

def: a doctor's forecast of the likely course and outcome of a disease
why: It shapes treatment decisions and helps patients and families plan ahead.
ex: Because the cancer was caught early, the prognosis was very good.
The vet gave a hopeful prognosis for the injured dog's leg.

cloze.s: Once the tests identified Hannah's illness, her next question was about her ___: how it would likely progress.

note: A diagnosis identifies the illness; a prognosis predicts how it will go.

def: the vast community of bacteria, fungi and viruses living in and on a person's body, especially the gut
why: Research links it to digestion, immunity and many diseases, though much remains under study.
ex: A course of antibiotics can temporarily disrupt the gut microbiome.
Researchers are studying how diet shapes the microbiome of newborn babies.

cloze.s: Eating more fiber feeds the helpful bacteria that make up your gut ___.

def: the brain's ability to rewire itself by forming new connections in response to learning, experience or injury
why: It explains how stroke patients can regain skills and how adults keep learning throughout life.
ex: Thanks to neuroplasticity, Wei regained the use of his hand after months of therapy following a stroke.
Learning to play the violin as an adult is possible because of neuroplasticity.

cloze.s: Rehabilitation after a brain injury relies on ___, as healthy regions take over lost functions.

def: an infection that jumps from animals to humans, such as rabies or bird flu
why: Many emerging infections begin this way, so human, animal and environmental health are watched together.
ex: Rabies is a zoonotic disease usually spread through the bite of an infected animal.
Public health officials track bird flu closely because it is a zoonotic disease.

cloze.s: Because rabies passes from animals to people, it is classified as a ___.

def: an amount expressed as a part of 100, so 25 out of every 100 is written as 25%
why: Discounts, taxes, test scores, interest rates and poll results are all reported this way.
ex: The store advertised a 30% discount, so Liam worked out what percentage of the price he would actually pay.
What percentage of your monthly income goes to rent?

cloze.s: If 18 of the 24 students passed the exam, the passing ___ was 75%.

def: a number showing part of a whole, written as one number over another, like 3/4
why: Recipes, measurements, music and money all use them.
ex: Sofia's daughter learned that the fraction 1/2 is equal to 2/4.
Only a small fraction of the people who applied were invited to interview.

cloze.s: If you cut a pizza into eight slices and eat three, you have eaten the ___ 3/8 of it.

def: a comparison of two amounts showing how much of one there is for each unit of the other, like 2 to 1
why: Recipes, maps, staffing levels and finance all describe relationships this way.
ex: The recipe uses a ratio of two cups of water to one cup of rice.
The school promised a student-to-teacher ratio of 15 to 1.

cloze.s: The paint instructions call for a ___ of four parts paint to one part thinner.

def: any whole value above 1 whose only exact divisors are 1 and itself, such as 2, 3, 5 or 7
why: They are the building blocks of all whole numbers and underpin modern internet encryption.
ex: Jamal confirmed that 13 is a prime number because nothing but 1 and 13 divides it evenly.
Students are often surprised that 2 is the only even prime number.

cloze.s: Since 9 can be divided evenly by 3, it is not a ___.

def: the total distance around the outside edge of a shape
why: It is used for fencing, framing, trim and any job that follows an outer boundary.
ex: To fence the garden, Kwame added its sides, 12 meters plus 8 meters, and doubled them for a perimeter of 40.
Security guards patrolled the perimeter of the stadium before the game.

cloze.s: A square with sides of 5 feet has a ___ of 20 feet.

note: Perimeter measures the boundary; area measures the space inside it.

def: the ordinary average: add up all the values and divide by how many values there are
why: It is the most common kind of average, though a few extreme values can pull it far from typical.
ex: To find the mean of her test scores, Priya added them up and divided by five.
A few billionaires moving to town would raise the mean income without changing most people's paychecks.

cloze.s: Scores of 70, 80 and 120 have a ___ of 90, found by adding them and dividing by three.

note: Not the same as the median, the middle value; extreme values affect the mean much more.

def: the middle value when a set of numbers is lined up from smallest to largest
why: News reports often use it for incomes and home prices because a few extreme values do not distort it.
ex: The median home price is often reported instead of the mean, because a few mansions can skew the mean upward.
Hannah sorted the nine test scores and found the median by picking the fifth one.

cloze.s: For the values 2, 4, 9, 50 and 100, the ___ is 9, the one in the middle.

note: With an even number of values, it is the mean of the two middle ones.

def: in statistics, the value that appears most often in a set of data
why: It is useful for finding the most common shoe size, survey answer or category.
ex: The mode of the shoe sizes sold that week was 9, so the store ordered more of them.
In the coffee survey, the mode was "two cups a day," the answer people gave most.

cloze.s: In the data 2, 2, 2, 5, 9 and 10, the ___ is 2 because it occurs most often.

def: how likely an event is to happen, expressed as a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain)
why: It underlies weather forecasts, insurance, medicine, games of chance and everyday risk decisions.
ex: The probability of rolling a six on a fair die is one in six.
The forecast gave a 70 percent probability of rain, so Diego packed an umbrella.

cloze.s: When you flip a fair coin, the ___ of getting heads is one half.

def: the simple arithmetic difference between two rates given out of 100, as when 10% rises to 12%
why: Confusing it with percent change makes news about interest rates, polls and taxes misleading.
ex: When the interest rate rose from 4% to 5%, it went up one percentage point, which is a 25% increase.
Support for the new park plan fell three percentage points, from 48% to 45%.

cloze.s: Unemployment rising from 5% to 6% is an increase of one ___, but a 20% relative increase.

note: A rise from 10% to 15% is 5 percentage points but a 50% increase.

def: a small raised number showing how many copies of a base are multiplied together, as in 2³ = 8
why: It is the language of compound growth, scientific notation and computer storage sizes.
ex: In the expression 10⁶, the exponent tells you to multiply six tens together to get one million.
Scientists use an exponent to write huge numbers compactly, such as 3 × 10⁸ meters per second for the speed of light.

cloze.s: In 5², the small raised 2 is the ___, so the answer is 25.

def: the value that, multiplied by itself, gives a particular number; for example, 3 for 9
why: It appears in geometry, physics formulas, statistics and the distance between two points.
ex: The square root of 64 is 8, because 8 times 8 equals 64.
Kwame took the square root of the room's 144 square feet to find that each wall of the square room was 12 feet long.

cloze.s: Because 12 × 12 = 144, the ___ of 144 is 12.

def: increase by a constant percentage each period, so the amount keeps doubling and accelerates rapidly
why: It explains how savings, populations and epidemics can seem slow at first and then explode.
ex: In exponential growth, a bacteria colony that doubles every hour goes from 1 cell to over 1,000 in ten hours.
Early in an outbreak, cases can show exponential growth, doubling every few days.

cloze.s: A rumor that each person passes to two new people every day spreads by ___, not by steady addition.

note: Not the same as linear growth, which adds a fixed amount each period.

def: the ratio of a circle's distance around to its width across, about 3.14159, written with the Greek letter π
why: It is used to calculate the area and circumference of circles, from pizza sizes to wheel designs.
ex: To find the circumference of the wheel, Yuki multiplied its diameter by pi.
Pi is an irrational number, so its decimal digits go on forever without repeating.

cloze.s: A circle's area equals ___ times the radius squared.

def: in algebra, a letter such as x that stands for an unknown or changing number
why: It is the basic tool of algebra, spreadsheets, computer programming and scientific experiments.
ex: In the equation 3x + 2 = 11, the variable x equals 3.
In the experiment, temperature was the only variable that Olga changed.

cloze.s: In the formula A = l × w for a rectangle's area, each letter is a ___ standing for a measurement.

def: a tenfold step in size, so something about 100 times bigger is two of these steps larger
why: Scientists and analysts use it to compare very different scales quickly.
ex: A city of a million people is an order of magnitude larger than a town of 100,000.
The new chip was an order of magnitude faster, finishing in one second what used to take ten.

cloze.s: Ten dollars and a hundred dollars differ by one ___.

def: a data point that sits far from all the others, unusually high or low compared with the rest
why: A single one can badly distort an average, so analysts check for them before drawing conclusions.
ex: One customer's $10,000 order was an outlier that made the store's average sale look far bigger.
Kwame's 45-point game was an outlier in a season when he usually scored about 15.

cloze.s: Most temperatures that month were near 70°F, but one reading of 20°F was an ___ caused by a broken sensor.

note: Figuratively, a person or thing very different from the rest of its group.

def: any whole number, positive, negative or zero, with no fraction or decimal part
why: Counting, temperatures below zero and computer programming all rely on them.
ex: Mateo explained that −5, 0 and 12 are each an integer, but 2.5 is not.
The spreadsheet rejected 3.7 because that box only accepts an integer.

cloze.s: The answer must be an ___, so 4 is allowed but 4.5 is not.

def: a measure of how spread out values are around their average; small means clustered, large means widely scattered
why: It is used to judge the reliability of data, investment risk and whether a result is unusual.
ex: Both classes averaged 75, but one had a much larger standard deviation in scores.
Investors treat the standard deviation of returns as one measure of a stock's risk.

cloze.s: The players on the team were all nearly the same height, so the ___ of their heights was very small.

def: a judgment that a result is unlikely to be due to chance alone, usually using a threshold like p < 0.05
why: Research headlines depend on it, but a result can pass this test and still be tiny or unimportant in practice.
ex: The drug's benefit reached statistical significance, but it shortened colds by only half a day.
Researchers warned that a single study's statistical significance does not prove a finding is true.

cloze.s: The small difference between the two groups did not reach ___, so it may have been due to chance.

note: "Significant" here does not mean important; it means unlikely to be explained by chance alone.

def: the power to which a base must be raised to produce a given number; with base 10, 1,000 gives 3
why: Scales for earthquakes, sound (decibels) and acidity (pH) are built on them.
ex: The base-10 logarithm of 1,000 is 3, because 10 × 10 × 10 equals 1,000.
Because the Richter scale uses a logarithm, each whole step means ten times greater ground motion.

cloze.s: Decibels are based on a ___, so each 10-decibel increase means ten times the sound intensity.

def: the range above and below a survey result within which the true value probably lies
why: It tells you how much to trust a poll; two results within this range may not truly differ.
ex: The poll showed 52 percent support with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points.
Since the gap was smaller than the margin of error, analysts said the race was too close to call.

cloze.s: A survey of only 100 people has a larger ___ than an otherwise similar survey of 2,000 people.

def: a mean that gives some values more influence than others, such as a final exam counting double
why: Course grades, grade point averages, stock indexes and price indexes are calculated this way.
ex: Her course grade is a weighted average in which the final exam counts for 40 percent.
A grade point average is a weighted average, since courses with more credits count more.

cloze.s: Because homework is worth 20% and exams 80%, the teacher computes a ___ rather than a simple mean.

def: the product of a whole number and every positive whole number below it, written with an exclamation mark: 4! = 24
why: It is used to count arrangements and combinations, from seating charts to lottery odds.
ex: Five books can be arranged on a shelf in 5 factorial, or 120, different orders.
Tomás was amazed that 10 factorial is more than three and a half million.

cloze.s: The number of ways to line up 6 people is 6 ___, which equals 720.

def: a rule for revising the probability of something in light of new evidence, starting from how likely it was before
why: It explains why a positive result on a test for a rare disease is often a false alarm.
ex: Using Bayes' theorem, the doctor explained why a positive screening test did not mean Priya surely had the rare disease.
Spam filters have long used Bayes' theorem to judge whether an email is junk.

cloze.s: To update the chance of rain after spotting dark clouds, a forecaster could apply ___.

def: a symmetrical, bell-shaped pattern of data in which most values cluster near the average and extremes are rare
why: Heights, measurement errors and test scores often roughly follow it, and many statistical methods assume it.
ex: Adult heights roughly follow a normal distribution, with few very short or very tall people.
In a normal distribution, about 68 percent of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean.

cloze.s: Plotted on a graph, the test scores formed a ___, the classic symmetrical bell curve.

def: the tendency for an extreme result to be followed by one closer to average, simply by chance
why: It explains why a slump often improves after any change, fooling people into crediting the change.
ex: After his record-breaking month, Liam's sales dipped, a classic case of regression to the mean.
Patients often seek treatment when symptoms peak, so regression to the mean can make useless remedies seem to work.

cloze.s: The team's unusually long losing streak ended on its own, which statisticians attribute to ___.

def: a value that cannot be written as a fraction of two integers; its decimal digits go on forever without repeating
why: Pi and the square root of 2 are famous examples, showing that not every quantity is a neat ratio.
ex: The square root of 2 is an irrational number, so its decimal expansion never settles into a pattern.
Since pi is an irrational number, any decimal value you use for it is only an approximation.

cloze.s: Because its decimals never end or repeat, the square root of 2 is an ___.

def: the series 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13…, where each term is the sum of the previous two
why: It turns up in math puzzles, computer science and some plant patterns, such as the spirals in seed heads.
ex: The number of spirals in a sunflower head is often a number from the Fibonacci sequence.
Malik wrote a short program that printed the first 20 numbers of the Fibonacci sequence.

cloze.s: In the ___, the number after 8 is 13, because 5 + 8 = 13.

note: Its popular link to the "golden ratio" in art and architecture is often exaggerated.

def: the principle that as a random trial is repeated more times, the average result gets closer to the expected value
why: It is why casinos and insurers can predict their totals reliably even though single events are random.
ex: Ten coin flips may give seven heads, but by the law of large numbers, 10,000 flips will land near half heads.
Insurance companies rely on the law of large numbers to predict how many claims they will pay each year.

cloze.s: A casino may lose to a lucky player tonight, but the ___ practically guarantees it profits over millions of bets.

note: It does not mean a streak must soon "balance out"; that belief is the gambler's fallacy.

def: the programs and apps that tell a computer, phone or other device what to do
why: Everyday devices, from cars to thermostats, depend on it and on regular updates.
ex: Wei updated the software on his laptop to fix a security flaw.
The accounting team switched to new software for tracking expenses.

cloze.s: The computer itself worked fine, but the ___ kept crashing whenever Maria opened a large file.

def: the physical parts of a computer or electronic device, such as the screen, keyboard and chips
why: Knowing the difference from programs helps you troubleshoot problems and buy devices wisely.
ex: The laptop's hardware was fine; the problem was a buggy app.
Jamal upgraded his hardware by adding more memory to his desktop computer.

cloze.s: When the phone's screen cracked, the repair shop said it was a ___ problem, not an app issue.

note: Also means tools and building supplies, as in a hardware store.

def: an app such as Chrome, Safari or Firefox used to find, open and view pages on the internet
why: It is the main window to the internet, so keeping it updated matters for security.
ex: Sofia opened her web browser and typed in the airline's address to check her flight.
If a page will not load properly, try clearing your web browser's history and cookies.

cloze.s: To visit a website on a laptop, you first open a ___ such as Firefox or Safari.

def: wireless technology that uses radio waves to connect phones, laptops and other devices to the internet or a local network
why: Homes, offices, airports and cafés rely on it, and public networks carry security risks.
ex: The café offers free Wi-Fi, so Kwame works there on Fridays.
Hannah moved the router upstairs to improve the Wi-Fi signal in her bedroom.

cloze.s: The hotel gave each guest a password to join its ___ network.

note: Despite a popular belief, the name does not officially stand for "wireless fidelity."

def: the core software, such as Windows, macOS, Android or iOS, that runs a device and its apps
why: It determines which apps you can use and needs regular updates to stay secure.
ex: Diego's phone needed an operating system update before the new app would install.
Most office computers run the same operating system so IT staff can manage them easily.

cloze.s: Windows and macOS are each an ___ that manages a computer's memory, files and apps.

def: an online service, such as Google or Bing, that finds web pages matching the words you type
why: Knowing how results are ranked, including paid ads, helps you judge what you find.
ex: Aisha typed her symptoms into a search engine but then called her doctor for real advice.
Some of the top results on a search engine are paid advertisements.

cloze.s: Liam typed his question into a ___, which ranked thousands of matching pages and showed the top ten.

def: a precise set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, often by computer
why: These rules shape what you see on social media, search results, loan decisions and route directions.
ex: The app's algorithm recommends videos based on what you watched before.
A recipe is like an algorithm: follow the steps in order and you get the same result.

cloze.s: The navigation app uses an ___ to calculate the fastest route through traffic.

def: using storage, software and processing power on remote servers over the internet instead of on your own device
why: Email, photo backups, streaming and most business software now run this way.
ex: With cloud computing, Olga's company stopped buying its own servers and rented capacity online instead.
Thanks to cloud computing, Malik can open his work files from any device.

cloze.s: Storing your photos on remote servers rather than on your phone is an example of ___.

def: harmful software, such as viruses, ransomware or spyware, designed to damage devices or steal data
why: It can lock files, steal passwords and spread through email attachments or fake downloads.
ex: The IT department warned that the strange attachment contained malware.
Yuki's antivirus program caught malware hidden in a free game download.

cloze.s: After clicking a suspicious link, Tomás discovered ___ that secretly recorded every key he typed.

def: a scam using fake emails, texts or websites to trick people into revealing passwords or financial details
why: It is one of the most common ways that people and companies get hacked.
ex: The email looked like it came from Priya's bank, but it was a phishing attempt.
Our company runs regular training so employees can spot phishing messages.

cloze.s: An email claiming your account is locked and asking you to "verify your password here" is a classic ___ scam.

def: a login safeguard requiring a second proof of identity, such as a texted code, in addition to a password
why: It blocks many account takeovers even when a password has been stolen.
ex: After turning on two-factor authentication, Jamal had to enter a code from his phone each time he logged in.
The bank now requires two-factor authentication for all online transfers.

cloze.s: Even though hackers stole her password, ___ stopped them because they lacked the code sent to her phone.

note: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is the broader term for requiring two or more checks.

def: the maximum amount of data a network connection can carry in a given time
why: It determines how smoothly you can stream video, join calls or download files.
ex: Streaming movies in 4K takes much more bandwidth than standard video.
When the whole family was on video calls at once, the home network did not have enough bandwidth.

cloze.s: The office upgraded its internet plan to get more ___, so large files would download faster.

note: Informally, a person's capacity or time: "I don't have the bandwidth for another project."

def: scrambling information into a code so that only someone with the right key can read it
why: It protects online banking, shopping, messaging and stored passwords.
ex: The padlock icon in your browser shows that encryption is protecting the connection.
Hospitals use encryption to keep patient records safe if a laptop is stolen.

cloze.s: Thanks to ___, a thief who intercepts the data sees only scrambled characters.

def: computer systems that perform tasks normally requiring human thinking, such as recognizing speech, translating or making decisions
why: It powers voice assistants, recommendations and chatbots, and raises questions about jobs and accuracy.
ex: The radiology clinic uses artificial intelligence to flag scans for a doctor to review.
Olga used an artificial intelligence tool to translate a letter from Portuguese.

cloze.s: The term ___ was coined in the 1950s for the broad goal of building machines that can think.

def: programs whose underlying code is publicly available for anyone to use, study, change and share
why: Much of the internet, including Linux and many web tools, is built on it.
ex: The nonprofit saved money by using open-source software for its website.
Firefox and Linux are well-known examples of open-source software.

cloze.s: Because the program is ___, any developer can read its code and suggest improvements.

def: a security barrier, in hardware or software, that monitors network traffic and blocks unauthorized access
why: It is a basic defense for home routers and company networks against intruders.
ex: The company's firewall blocked thousands of suspicious connection attempts every day.
Kwame's game would not connect until he allowed it through his computer's firewall.

cloze.s: The IT team set up a ___ to stop outside traffic from reaching the office network.

def: a numerical label identifying a device on a network so that data reaches the right destination
why: Websites and streaming services use it to estimate your location, and networks use it to route data.
ex: Websites can often guess which city you are in from your IP address.
The home router assigns each phone and laptop in the house its own IP address.

cloze.s: Every device that connects to the internet uses an ___, a numeric label such as 192.168.1.1.

note: IP stands for Internet Protocol.

def: a satellite-based navigation system that pinpoints a receiver's location anywhere on Earth
why: Phone maps, delivery tracking, aviation and even precise timing for networks depend on it.
ex: Without cell service, the hikers used GPS to find their way back to the trail.
The delivery app uses GPS to show exactly where the driver is.

cloze.s: The car's ___ receiver calculated its position from signals sent by orbiting satellites.

note: Stands for Global Positioning System, run by the U.S.; other countries operate similar satellite systems.

def: a type of AI in which computers improve at a task by finding patterns in data rather than following hand-written rules
why: It drives spam filters, recommendations, fraud detection and medical image analysis.
ex: The bank uses machine learning to spot unusual purchases that might be fraud.
Priya's research team trained a machine learning model on thousands of heart scans.

cloze.s: Instead of programming every rule, the engineers used ___ so the system could pick up spam patterns from millions of examples.

def: a material such as silicon whose ability to carry electric current can be controlled, used to make computer chips
why: Nearly all electronics depend on them, so their supply affects cars, phones and whole economies.
ex: Every smartphone contains semiconductor chips that store and process information.
A shortage of semiconductor chips delayed car production around the world in 2021.

cloze.s: Silicon is the most widely used ___ in computer chips.

def: a shared digital record of transactions, copied across many computers and linked so past entries are very hard to alter
why: It is the technology behind cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and some supply-chain tracking systems.
ex: Bitcoin transactions are recorded on a public blockchain that anyone can inspect.
The shipping company tested a blockchain to track containers from port to port.

cloze.s: Bitcoin relies on a ___, a ledger maintained by thousands of computers rather than a single bank.

def: a defined set of rules that lets one software program request data or services from another
why: Weather apps, online payments and embedded maps all work by calling other companies' services this way.
ex: The travel site uses an airline's API to show live flight prices.
Diego's fitness app pulls the day's weather forecast through a free API.

cloze.s: To show maps inside its own app, the delivery company connects to a mapping service's ___.

note: Stands for application programming interface.

def: the delay between sending a signal or request and getting a response, often measured in milliseconds
why: Keeping it low matters for video calls, online gaming and financial trading.
ex: High latency made Sofia's video call lag, so people kept talking over each other.
Gamers often prefer wired connections because they usually offer lower latency than Wi-Fi.

cloze.s: Even with a fast download speed, the satellite connection had high ___, causing a noticeable delay on calls.

note: Not the same as bandwidth: latency is delay, while bandwidth is capacity.

def: the observation that the number of transistors on a computer chip roughly doubles about every two years
why: It explains decades of rapidly cheaper, faster electronics, though the pace has slowed.
ex: Thanks to Moore's law, a phone today is far more powerful than the room-sized computers of the 1960s.
Engineers debate how much longer Moore's law can continue as transistors approach the size of atoms.

cloze.s: The steady doubling of transistors on chips over several decades is known as ___.

note: An observed trend, not a law of nature; Intel co-founder Gordon Moore first described it in 1965.

def: a computer model loosely inspired by the brain, made of layers of connected units that learn patterns from data
why: It is the core technology behind modern image recognition, speech recognition and chatbots.
ex: The neural network learned to recognize cats after training on millions of photos.
Hannah's thesis used a neural network to predict crop yields from satellite images.

cloze.s: Like a simplified brain, the ___ passes data through layers of connected nodes to recognize handwriting.

def: information processing with qubits, which can exist in a mix of 0 and 1, promising big speedups on certain problems
why: If it matures, it could break much of today's encryption and speed up chemistry and materials research.
ex: Security experts worry that quantum computing could someday crack the encryption that protects bank data.
Several tech companies are racing to build practical quantum computing systems.

cloze.s: Because qubits can hold a blend of 0 and 1, ___ may solve some problems that ordinary chips cannot handle in practice.

def: a proposed trial in which a machine passes if a human judge, chatting by text, cannot reliably tell it from a person
why: It is a classic benchmark in debates over whether machines can think.
ex: Alan Turing proposed what became known as the Turing test in a 1950 paper on machine intelligence.
Critics argue that passing the Turing test shows a chatbot can imitate conversation, not that it understands.

cloze.s: If judges chatting by text cannot tell whether they are talking to a computer or a person, the computer has passed the ___.

note: Turing himself called it the "imitation game."

def: a way of securing messages so only the sender and recipient can read them, not even the service provider
why: It protects private chats and calls in messaging apps such as Signal and WhatsApp.
ex: Because the app uses end-to-end encryption, the company itself cannot read users' messages.
Wei switched to a messaging service with end-to-end encryption to protect his conversations.

cloze.s: With ___, a message is locked on the sender's phone and unlocked only on the recipient's, so not even the company's servers can read it.

def: an AI system trained on huge amounts of text to predict and generate humanlike writing
why: These systems power modern chatbots and writing tools, which are useful but can state false information confidently.
ex: The customer-service chatbot runs on a large language model that drafts replies in seconds.
Teachers discussed how students might use a large language model to brainstorm essay topics.

cloze.s: Trained on billions of words, the ___ could summarize reports and draft emails, though it occasionally invented facts.

def: a software security flaw unknown to its maker, so no fix exists when attackers first exploit it
why: These flaws are prized by criminals and spies because they work before any defense is available.
ex: Hackers used a zero-day vulnerability in the browser to break into hundreds of computers before a patch was released.
The company rushed out an emergency update after researchers reported a zero-day vulnerability.

cloze.s: Attackers exploited a ___ in the phone's software, a flaw the manufacturer had not yet discovered or patched.

def: distance north or south of the equator, measured in degrees from 0 to 90
why: It strongly shapes climate and day length, and it is half of every map coordinate.
ex: Chicago and Rome sit at a similar latitude, about 42 degrees north.
In summer, places at a higher latitude get longer days than places near the equator.

cloze.s: The equator has a ___ of 0 degrees, and the North Pole is at 90 degrees north.

note: Lines of latitude run east-west; lines of longitude run north-south.

def: distance east or west of the prime meridian in Greenwich, England, measured in degrees from 0 to 180
why: Paired with the north-south coordinate, it pinpoints any spot on Earth and relates to time zones.
ex: Sailors long struggled to find their longitude at sea until accurate clocks were invented.
The GPS showed the hikers' position, including a longitude of 105 degrees west.

cloze.s: Greenwich, England, sits on the prime meridian, at 0 degrees ___.

def: one of Earth's few very large landmasses, such as Africa, Asia or South America
why: Geography, climate, history and travel are often discussed in terms of these big divisions.
ex: Antarctica is the coldest continent and has no permanent residents.
Australia is often described as the only country that covers an entire continent.

cloze.s: Africa is the second-largest ___ on Earth by both area and population.

note: Different traditions count five, six or seven continents.

def: the imaginary circle around Earth's middle, halfway between the North and South Poles
why: It divides the planet into Northern and Southern hemispheres, and lowlands near it stay warm year-round.
ex: Ecuador takes its name from the equator, which passes through the country.
Near the equator, day and night are each about 12 hours long all year.

cloze.s: Kenya and Brazil are both crossed by the ___, so each lies partly in the Northern and partly in the Southern Hemisphere.

def: the typical weather of a region measured over many years, including average temperature and rainfall
why: It shapes what crops grow, how homes are built and where people choose to live.
ex: Arizona's desert climate means hot summers and very little rain.
Olga moved from Phoenix to Seattle and had to adjust to a much rainier climate.

cloze.s: One snowy day in April says little about a region's ___, which is measured over decades.

note: Weather is short-term conditions, like today's rain; climate is the long-term pattern.

def: one half of Earth, divided either by the equator into north and south or by a meridian into east and west
why: Seasons are reversed between the northern and southern halves, so July is winter in Australia.
ex: When it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere, it is winter in the Southern Hemisphere.
Most of the world's people live in the Northern Hemisphere.

cloze.s: Australia, Argentina and South Africa all lie in the southern ___.

def: the theory that Earth's outer shell is broken into huge slabs that slowly move, causing earthquakes and building mountains
why: It explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain ranges and why continents drift apart.
ex: Plate tectonics explains why Iceland is slowly being pulled apart along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
The Himalayas formed through plate tectonics as India collided with the rest of Asia.

cloze.s: Earthquakes in California occur because of ___, as two enormous slabs of Earth's crust grind past each other.

def: the warming of Earth's surface caused by gases such as carbon dioxide trapping heat in the atmosphere
why: Naturally it keeps Earth livable; extra gases from burning fossil fuels strengthen it and drive global warming.
ex: Without the natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be well below freezing.
Venus is hotter than Mercury because of its extreme greenhouse effect.

cloze.s: Carbon dioxide and methane add to the ___ by trapping heat near Earth's surface.

def: the gradual wearing away and removal of soil and rock by water, wind or ice
why: It shapes landscapes like the Grand Canyon and threatens farmland, beaches and coastal homes.
ex: Erosion by the Colorado River over millions of years helped carve the Grand Canyon.
Farmers planted rows of trees along the field edges to reduce soil erosion from wind.

cloze.s: Waves pounding the cliffs caused so much ___ that several houses had to be moved inland.

note: Figuratively, a gradual loss: "the erosion of trust."

def: the regular rise and fall of sea level, usually about twice a day, caused mainly by the Moon's gravity
why: Boaters, fishers and beachgoers plan around it, and it affects coastal flooding.
ex: At low tide, Maria and her kids explored the rock pools on the beach.
The fishing boat waited for high tide before crossing the shallow harbor entrance.

cloze.s: The beach nearly disappeared at high ___, so they waited a few hours for the water to go back out.

def: a fan-shaped area of land formed where a river deposits sediment as it enters a sea or lake
why: These areas, like the Nile's and the Mississippi's, are fertile and densely farmed but vulnerable to flooding.
ex: The Nile delta has been farmed for thousands of years because of its rich soil.
Rising seas threaten the many communities living on the low-lying Mekong Delta.

cloze.s: Before reaching the Gulf of Mexico, the Mississippi River spreads into a marshy ___ of channels and islands.

note: Named after the Greek letter Δ, whose triangle shape resembles the Nile's.

def: a region of Earth whose clocks all show the same standard hour, usually one hour off from neighboring regions
why: They matter for travel, scheduling meetings and running global businesses.
ex: Chicago is one time zone behind New York, so a 9 a.m. call in Chicago is 10 a.m. in New York.
China uses a single time zone even though the country is wide enough to span several.

cloze.s: Kwame landed in London and reset his watch to match the new ___.

def: long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns, now driven mainly by human activity, especially burning fossil fuels
why: It affects sea levels, heat waves, farming and public policy around the world.
ex: Scientists link climate change to rising sea levels as glaciers melt and warming oceans expand.
Wine growers are planting different grape varieties as climate change brings hotter summers.

cloze.s: Shrinking Arctic sea ice and rising average temperatures over decades are major signs of ___.

note: Global warming is the temperature rise itself; this term also covers broader effects. One cold winter does not disprove the long-term trend.

def: a band of gas in the upper atmosphere that absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays
why: Its thinning led to a successful global treaty phasing out the chemicals that damaged it.
ex: Chemicals once used in spray cans and refrigerators damaged the ozone layer.
Scientists report that the ozone layer has been slowly recovering since harmful chemicals were phased out.

cloze.s: The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out chemicals that were thinning the ___, especially over Antarctica.

note: Ozone depletion and climate change are largely separate problems, though they are often confused.

def: a seasonal shift in winds that brings a long rainy season, especially to South Asia
why: Its rains are vital to farming and water supplies for over a billion people, and can also cause floods.
ex: Farmers in India time their planting around the arrival of the monsoon.
The monsoon brought weeks of heavy rain, flooding streets across Mumbai.

cloze.s: Every summer, the ___ winds carry moist ocean air over India, bringing months of heavy rain.

def: a cold, treeless region with frozen subsoil and short summers, found in the Arctic and on high mountains
why: These fragile regions hold vast amounts of carbon in frozen soil, and the Arctic is warming faster than most of the planet.
ex: Caribou migrate across the Arctic tundra in huge herds.
Only low plants such as mosses and lichens grow on the windswept tundra.

cloze.s: No trees grow on the frozen ___ of northern Alaska, only mosses, lichens and small shrubs.

def: an area of land where all rain and snowmelt drain into the same river, lake or bay
why: Pollution anywhere in this area can end up in the water supply downstream.
ex: Fertilizer runoff from farms across the watershed harmed the lake's fish.
Much of the central United States lies in the Mississippi River watershed, so its rain ends up in the Gulf of Mexico.

cloze.s: Protecting the forests throughout the ___ keeps the streams feeding the city's reservoir clean.

note: Figuratively, a turning point: "a watershed moment."

def: an underground layer of rock, sand or gravel that holds water that can be pumped up through wells
why: Many cities and farms depend on them, and pumping faster than they refill can drain them.
ex: The Ogallala aquifer supplies water to farms across the Great Plains.
Overpumping the aquifer caused the ground above it to sink in parts of California.

cloze.s: The town's wells draw drinking water from an ___ deep beneath the valley floor.

def: a horseshoe-shaped zone around the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes and many volcanoes occur
why: It explains why Japan, Chile, Indonesia and the U.S. West Coast face frequent quakes and eruptions.
ex: Japan lies on the Ring of Fire, so its buildings are designed to withstand strong earthquakes.
Mount St. Helens is one of many volcanoes along the Ring of Fire.

cloze.s: Most of the planet's active volcanoes are found along the Pacific's ___.

def: a periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific that disrupts weather worldwide
why: It can bring droughts, floods and unusual temperatures to many regions, affecting crops and food prices.
ex: During an El Niño winter, the southern United States often gets more rain than usual.
Fishermen in Peru noticed the warm El Niño waters around Christmas, which gave the event its name.

cloze.s: Forecasters warned that ___, the warming of Pacific waters, could bring heavy rains to Peru and drought to Australia.

note: Its opposite phase, with cooler-than-normal Pacific waters, is La Niña.

def: a fast, narrow band of wind high in the atmosphere that flows west to east and steers weather systems
why: It guides storms and cold snaps, and pilots use it to shorten eastbound flights.
ex: Flights from New York to London are often shorter because they ride the jet stream.
A dip in the jet stream let Arctic air pour south into the Midwest.

cloze.s: Eastbound planes over the Atlantic save fuel by riding the ___, a band of fast winds high above the clouds.

def: a crack in Earth's crust where blocks of rock have moved past each other, often causing earthquakes
why: Knowing where they lie guides building codes and earthquake preparation.
ex: California's San Andreas is a fault line that runs for hundreds of miles.
Engineers refused to build the new hospital directly on top of the fault line.

cloze.s: The earthquake struck when rocks along the ___ suddenly slipped several feet.

note: Also used figuratively for a deep division within a group or society.

def: the apparent deflection of moving air and water caused by Earth's rotation, curving right north of the equator
why: It makes large storms spin and shapes global wind and ocean current patterns.
ex: Because of the Coriolis effect, hurricanes in the Northern Hemisphere spin counterclockwise.
Contrary to a popular myth, the Coriolis effect is far too weak to decide which way a sink drains.

cloze.s: Hurricanes south of the equator spin clockwise because of the ___.

def: ground that stays frozen for at least two years in a row, common in Arctic regions
why: As it thaws, buildings and roads buckle and stored carbon can be released into the air.
ex: Thawing permafrost has caused roads and houses in Alaska to crack and tilt.
Scientists found ancient mammoth remains preserved in Siberian permafrost.

cloze.s: In northern Canada, ground called ___ stays frozen all year, even beneath the thawed summer topsoil.

def: a proposed name for the current period in which human activity is a dominant influence on Earth's climate and ecosystems
why: The term frames discussions of humanity's lasting mark on the planet, from plastics to extinctions.
ex: Some scientists call our era the Anthropocene because humans now reshape the planet.
Layers of plastic and concrete could serve as markers of the Anthropocene in future rock records.

cloze.s: Geologists debated whether to name a new epoch, the ___, defined by humanity's impact on Earth.

note: In 2024, geology's official panel declined to adopt it as a formal epoch, though the term remains widely used.

def: a narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses, with water on both sides
why: Canals are often cut through them, as at Panama and Suez, reshaping world trade.
ex: The Panama Canal was built across the Isthmus of Panama to link the Atlantic and Pacific.
A narrow canal cuts across the isthmus of Corinth in Greece.

cloze.s: Central America forms an ___ joining North and South America.

note: Its water counterpart, a narrow channel joining two larger bodies of water, is a strait.

def: a dry area on the downwind side of a mountain range, where moist air has already lost its moisture
why: It explains why deserts and dry valleys sit right beside lush, rainy mountains.
ex: Eastern Washington is dry because it lies in the rain shadow of the Cascade Mountains.
Death Valley sits in the rain shadow of the Sierra Nevada and other ranges.

cloze.s: The coast is lush, but the land beyond the mountains is a desert because it sits in a ___.

def: the supercontinent that joined nearly all of Earth's land before it began breaking apart roughly 200 million years ago
why: It explains why the coasts of Africa and South America fit together like puzzle pieces.
ex: Matching fossils found on different continents helped scientists reconstruct Pangaea.
Over many millions of years, Pangaea split apart into the continents we know today.

cloze.s: When the first dinosaurs appeared, Earth's landmasses were joined in a single supercontinent called ___.

note: Also spelled Pangea.

def: how much sunlight a surface reflects, from fresh snow reflecting most to dark ocean absorbing most
why: Melting ice lowers it, making Earth absorb more heat and speeding warming.
ex: Fresh snow has a very high albedo, which is why it can be blinding on sunny days.
As sea ice melts, the darker ocean's lower albedo lets it soak up more of the sun's heat.

cloze.s: Cities paint roofs white to raise their ___ and keep buildings cooler in summer.

def: the wide mouth of a river where fresh water mixes with salty tidal water from the sea
why: These mixing zones are nurseries for many fish and shellfish and are often busy ports.
ex: The Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States.
Young salmon spend time in the estuary adjusting to salt water before heading out to sea.

cloze.s: Where the river meets the sea, its brackish ___ supports oyster beds and young fish.
